newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX crude futures turn lower on profit-taking.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX crude futures turn lower on profit-taking.

text.p: Crude oil and product futures remained choppy on the NYMEX Thursday and were showing slight gains in early afternoon trading.
November crude futures were up 13 cents at $25.30 a barrel at 1400 EDT, having traded a $24.90-$25.54 range.
Early strength was due to a bullish Energy Information Agency weekly report on inventories, but the market remains nervous after the strong bull run, traders said.
"I'm bearish for the market right now," said Thomas Blakeslee, a trader/analyst at Cargill Investors Service.
"I think you'll see heating oil push back below 70 (cents a gallon) and I wouldn't be surpised to see that before tomorrow's close," Blakeslee added.
November heating oil was down a point at 71.55 cents a gallon just after 1400 EDT but had been swinging back and forth for most of the session.

The contract shot up to 74.40 on Wednesday after another drop in American Petroleum Institute weekly heating oil inventories in the key northeast U.S. area, but then turned sharply lower to hit a low of 70.75.
Thursday's recovery was helped by the EIA data showing a 3.3 million barrel draw on crude stocks and a 900,000 barrel drop in distillate stocks.

However, there have been worries that the heating oil market, after rising 50 pct in the past three-and-a-half months and leading the energy complex up, might be hit if the Department of Energy tries to curb the price gains in order to cushion the blow to consumers this winter.
Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary is due to meet oil company executives on Friday to discuss the issue.
The possibility of any substantial action by the government was widely ruled out by analysts over the past couple of days, nevertheless a number still feel the market is vulnerable to a setback.
"People are a little scared of the meeting tomorrow but most believe that politicians really don't have much ability to do anything," said Blakeslee.

There may be potential for real action later in the year if consumers are facing rises maybe 30 pct above current levels, but in the meantime all the speculators and commercial interests appear to have bought as much as they want, thus leaving the market vulnerable to a setback, Blakeslee adds.
